# Anthropic is putting 5% of its shares into a public-benefit fund — here is what that means


By OpenTools Team


Anthropic says a new company‑owned fund will receive 5% of its shares, subject to stockholder approval, and could grow as the company’s value rises. The pledge could become substantial, but its dollar value, governance and first distributions remain undisclosed.


##


The commitment is equity, not a $5 cash donation


Anthropic[announced](https://www.anthropic.com/news/public-benefit-fund) on October 18 that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval. The company says the fund will be a wholly owned limited‑liability company rather than a conventional nonprofit.


That distinction matters. Five percent describes a stake in the company, not 5% of revenue, profit or cash on hand. Anthropic did not publish the number of shares, the valuation baseline or a dollar value for the stake. It also did not say whether the shares will be transferred from an existing holder or issued in another way, so the announcement alone does not establish dilution for current stockholders.


For readers, the clearest interpretation is a contingent pool of company equity. Its eventual value depends on Anthropic's valuation, the final approved structure and what the fund can realize or distribute.


##


The stake can grow when Anthropic's value rises


Anthropic says its board may add another 2% of shares for every 50% increase in the company's value above an undisclosed baseline. The word “may” is important: those additions are discretionary, not automatic.


The formula also cannot yet be converted into dates or dollar amounts. Anthropic has not disclosed the starting valuation used for this mechanism or the precise milestones. The company says it will publish more about the valuation milestones and fund governance in the coming months.


The result is an escalating commitment in percentage terms, with two unresolved gates: stockholder approval for the initial 5%, and board decisions for later additions.


##


Anthropic says the fund could address disruption from AI


The company gives two examples of what the fund might do: make large donations to established nonprofits or distribute money directly to particular groups. It names labour‑market disruption as one possible focus and points to a separate $200 million commitment to study and address the effects of AI on work.


Those are examples, not funded programs announced today. Anthropic has not named recipients, eligibility rules, a budget, a timetable or a first grant. The company also says equity held by the fund will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the United States or abroad.


That leaves a wide possible range, from conventional grants to direct payments. Which path the fund chooses will determine whether the commitment mainly supports research and institutions or reaches workers and communities affected by AI adoption.


##


Anthropic counts earlier founder and employee pledges toward roughly 20%


Anthropic says its co‑founders pledged at the company's creation to donate 80% of their personal equity holdings. It also operates an equity‑donation matching program that about half of employees use. The company says those commitments plus the new fund mean roughly 20% of Anthropic shares are dedicated to public benefit.


That 20% is a company‑reported aggregate, not 20% owned by the new fund. It combines different promises made by the company, founders and employees, and the announcement does not provide a cap‑table reconciliation or independent audit.


The pledge arrives as Anthropic's commercial scale is also growing. OpenTools recently[examined the company's reported $26 billion revenue run rate](https://opentools.ai/news/anthropic-revenue-26-billion-run-rate-paid-workplace-growth) , while noting that a run rate is not recognized annual revenue. Both stories make the same basic point: large headline numbers need their denominator, conditions and missing disclosures attached.


##


Governance is the main unanswered question


Anthropic says the fund will be wholly owned by the company, which gives it flexibility across forms of giving. That also makes decision rights central: who selects projects, what conflicts rules apply, how performance is measured and whether outsiders can verify the fund's work.


[TechCrunch noted](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/18/anthropic-says-its-committing-5-of-its-shares-to-a-public-benefit-fund/) that Anthropic plans to provide more information about the structure and governance in the coming months. Anthropic also promises an upcoming public‑benefit report. Until those arrive, the announcement establishes an intended equity commitment and broad permitted uses, but not an independently assessable grant‑making institution.


The next useful evidence is therefore concrete: stockholder approval, the legal and voting structure, the initial share allocation, named decision‑makers, valuation milestones, first recipients and regular audited reporting. Those details will show whether the fund becomes a durable counterweight to AI's social costs or remains a large but hard‑to‑value corporate pledge.
